title: gallery
text:
The gallery demos live in rupaka/demos/ as JSON. They show what a good demo looks like, and the agent gives two of them to the model as examples. The data of the Sanskrit and jyotiṣa demos comes from the vedicreader and ganapati sources, not from memory:
import json
from rupaka.spec import *
from rupaka.spec import _gates
from rupaka.render import show, save, page
from rupaka.check import check, can_check, browser, in_thread

title: gallery
text:
The demos
Each demo has a gate. Here are the gate questions and the blocks of each demo.

g = gallery()
for k, s in g.items(): print(f"{k:24} {[b['type'] for b in s['blocks']]}\n{'':24} {next(_gates(s['blocks']))['prompt']}")

title: gallery
text:
Each demo is valid
validate finds no errors in any gallery demo.

test_eq({k: list(validate(s)) for k, s in g.items()}, {k: [] for k in g})

title: gallery
text:
The builder form
A notebook author can write the sandhi demo with the builders. The result is the same dict as the JSON file.

V = ['a', 'ā', 'i', 'ī', 'u', 'ū', 'ṛ', 'e', 'ai', 'o', 'au']
sd = g['vowel-sandhi']
d = demo('vowel-sandhi', 'Vowel sandhi', ask=sd['ask'], state=dict(a='a', b='i'), derive=[rules('sandhi', ['a', 'b'], 'join')],
         blocks=[row(wheel('a', V, 'End of word 1'), wheel('b', V, 'Start of word 2')),
                 gate('join', 'What do the two vowels become?', from_('join.alts'), 'join.out', context='For {a} + {b}:',
                      why='Say why, in one line, before you lock in.', again=True),
                 readout('{a} + {b} → {join.out}', label='The join', after='join'),
                 caption(sd['blocks'][3]['text'], after='join')],
         tables=sd['tables'])
test_eq(d, sd)

title: gallery
text:
The data
At 47°, the point is in Rohiṇī, pāda 3, in Vṛṣabha. At 30°, the start of Vṛṣabha, it is in Kṛttikā, pāda 2.

nk = g['nakshatra-pada']
test_eq(run(nk)['where'], 'Rohiṇī, pāda 3')
test_eq(run(nk)['rasi']['name'], 'Vṛṣabha')
test_eq(run(nk, dict(lon=30, show_pada=False))['where'], 'Kṛttikā, pāda 2')

For a + i, the join is e (guṇa). The wrong options come from the other rows of the table.

j = run(sd)['join']
test_eq((j['out'], j['name']), ('e', 'guṇa'))
test_eq(sorted(j['alts']), ['e', 'ā', 'ī', 'ū'])

With k = 60 the fused winner is B, which is in both lists. With k = 1 it is A, the top of one list.

rr = g['reciprocal-rank-fusion']
test_eq(run(rr)['fused'][0]['id'], 'B')
test_eq(run(rr, {**rr['state'], 'k': 1})['fused'][0]['id'], 'A')

title: render
text:
One runtime draws a spec everywhere. A host element carries the spec as inert JSON, and the runtime mounts it:
The runtime boots on load and after each htmx swap. Nothing is templated into the script.

title: render
text:
The bundle
bundle joins the core, the fns, the blocks and the boot script in a fixed order. The style sheet starts with paper.css, the tokens of the paper theme, which the side panel of the board (rupaka.board) uses too. There is no bundler and no build step.


source

bundle
def bundle(
    kind:str='js'
)->str:
The runtime as one script (js) or one style sheet (css), with this package’s version in the script. three gives three.js.




source

assets
def assets()->fastcore.basics.AttrDict:
The files of the runtime, in bundle order.


The script starts with the core and ends with the boot. Each block is in it.

js = bundle()
assert js.startswith('/* static/rupaka.js */') and js.rstrip().endswith('})();')
for n in manifests(): assert f"Rupaka.block('{n}'" in js, n
assert 'eval(' not in js and 'new Function' not in js and 'fetch(' not in js
assert f"version: '{__version__}'" in js and '{{version}}' not in js

Each block style uses only the --rk-* vars for colour, so a demo takes the look of the page that holds it.

import re


for p in assets().css[2:]:   # the blocks: paper.css and rupaka.css hold the colours
    cols = re.findall(r'(?:#[0-9a-fA-F]{3,6}\b|rgba?\(|hsl\()', p.read_text())
    test_eq((p.name, cols), (p.name, []))

title: render
text:
three.js for scenes
A scene block draws in 3D with three.js. rupaka keeps a copy of three.js in rupaka/static/vendor/three/, so a scene works offline and loads nothing from a CDN.







item
value




version
three 0.185.0, from npm (three-0.185.0.tgz, integrity sha512-+yRrcRO2iZa8uzvNNl0d7cL4huhgKgBvVJ0njcTe8xFqZ6DMAFZdCKDP91SEAuj25bNAj7k1QQdf+srZywVK6w==)


files
three.core.min.js and three.module.min.js, as npm gives them, with no change


licence
MIT, in vendor/three/LICENSE


size
about 750 KB



0.185.0 is the last release that has the minified files. The tests check the hash of each file, so a changed file fails at once.
The hashes of the two files, as sha256:

for f, h in THREE.files.items(): test_eq(hashlib.sha256((VENDOR/'three'/f).read_bytes()).hexdigest(), h)
assert 'MIT License' in (VENDOR/'three'/'LICENSE').read_text()

The two files are ES modules: the second one imports the first. A module cannot load from file:// or from a sandboxed srcdoc frame, and those are places where rupaka draws. So three_js joins the two files into one classic script. It changes only the import and export statements: an import becomes a read from the first file’s names, and an export becomes a return. The script puts the names on window.RupakaTHREE, and it does nothing when it runs a second time.


source

three_js
def three_js()->str:
three.js as one classic script that sets window.RupakaTHREE, made from the two vendored module files.


The script has no module statement left, and it exports the names that a scene uses.

t = three_js()
assert not re.search(r'(^|[;}])\s*(import|export)\s*[{*]', t) and 'from"./three' not in t
for k in ('WebGLRenderer', 'MeshToonMaterial', 'ExtrudeGeometry', 'DepthTexture', 'REVISION'): assert f'{k}:' in t, k
test_eq(bundle('three'), t)

needs gives the vendored libraries that a list of specs needs. Only a spec with a scene block needs three.js.


source

needs
def needs(
    specs
)->set:
The vendored libraries that specs need: three when a spec has a scene block.



test_eq(needs(dict(blocks=[dict(type='readout', text='x')])), set())
test_eq(needs([dict(blocks=[]), dict(blocks=[dict(type='stack', blocks=[dict(type='scene', blocks=[])])])]), {'three'})

source

host
def host(
    spec, theme:str=None, askable:bool=None

The host element: a div that carries its spec as inert JSON; theme='paper' gives it the paper look, askable the host switch.




source

spec_json
def spec_json(
    spec
)->str:
The spec as JSON that is safe inside a <script> element.



h = host(dict(id='x', ask='Do not stop at </script> here.'))
assert '</script>' not in h.split('<script type="application/json">')[1][:-len('</script></div>')]

title: render
text:
A static page
page writes one self-contained HTML file: the runtime, the style, the specs, and abhyasa’s palette. The fonts argument picks how the page gets its fonts:



fonts
what it does




'link'
links Literata, Libre Baskerville and the hand font Patrick Hand from ./fonts (save copies them)


'embed'
puts the fonts in the page as data URIs, about 220 KB more


'none'
uses the system serif; for a sandboxed srcdoc frame, which cannot load files





source

font_css
def font_css(
    fonts:str='link', base:str='fonts/'
)->str:
The @font-face rules: linked from base, embedded as data URIs, or none.


page takes one spec or a list of specs. A list makes a gallery page with a rule between the demos. When a spec has a scene, the page also holds three.js.


source

page
def page(
    specs, title:str=None, fonts:str='link', lead:str='', theme:str=None, askable:bool=None
)->str:
One self-contained HTML document that draws specs, with no network.


A page loads nothing from the network: no src, href or url() points at http. (The SVG namespace string is not a request.) With fonts='none' it has no @font-face rule.

spec = dict(rupaka=1, id='t', title='T', state=dict(a=1), blocks=[dict(type='readout', text='{a}')])
p = page(spec)
assert not re.search(r'''(src|href)=["']?https?:|url\(\s*["']?https?:''', p)
assert '@font-face' in p and '@font-face' not in page(spec, fonts='none')
assert 'data:font/woff2;base64,' in page(spec, fonts='embed')
assert 'window.RupakaTHREE=' not in p
s3 = page(dict(rupaka=1, id='s', state={}, blocks=[dict(type='scene', blocks=[])]), fonts='none')
assert 'window.RupakaTHREE=' in s3 and not re.search(r'''(src|href)=["']?https?:|url\(\s*["']?https?:''', s3)


The paper theme
The paper theme gives a demo a warm paper ground, light boxes, sketch lines and a hand font, as on a teacher’s board. It is always light. A host puts data-rk-theme="paper" on the demo element or on a parent. host, page and Demo take theme='paper'. The hand font is Patrick Hand, under the SIL Open Font License, in static/fonts with its licence. A host that serves the fonts loads it with font_css.

pp = page(spec, fonts='none', theme='paper')
assert '<div data-rupaka data-rk-theme="paper">' in pp and '<div data-rupaka>' in page(spec, fonts='none')
assert "font-family: 'Patrick Hand'" in font_css() and all((STATIC/'fonts'/f).exists() for *_, f, _ in FONTS)
assert 'Patrick Hand' in (STATIC/'fonts'/'LICENSES.txt').read_text()



Ask about this: the rk-ask event
Each demo shows a small “Ask about this” control at its end. The learner clicks it, can type a question, and clicks Ask (or pushes Enter). The demo then sends the rk-ask event, as a gate sends rk-predict. The event bubbles, crosses a shadow root and is cancelable. Its detail is plain JSON:



key
what it is




demo
the id of the spec


text
the words of the learner, at most 500 characters; it can be empty


state
the input keys (the keys of spec.state) and their values now, as Rupaka.state gives them. A string has at most 200 characters, and a list or an object at most 50 items, 3 levels deep.


step
the state key step of an explainer, else the id of the first open gate, else null



The event never holds derived values, gate answers, DOM or HTML. A host that takes the ask calls preventDefault. Then the demo says “Sent to the tutor.”, else “No tutor is on this page.” A host can send the same event with Rupaka.ask(el, text), for example from a voice command. It gives false when a listener called preventDefault.
The control is on by default. A spec turns it off with "askable": false. The host page can turn it on or off for one render, and the host switch comes first. For example, a talk shows the control in the editor but not in the window that the room sees. host, page and Demo take askable=True or askable=False, which writes data-rk-askable on the element. Rupaka.mount(el, spec, {askable}) does the same. With askable not set, the spec decides. In every case the event is the same.

assert '<div data-rupaka>' in page(spec, fonts='none')
assert '<div data-rupaka data-rk-askable="false">' in page(spec, fonts='none', askable=False)
assert '<div data-rupaka data-rk-theme="paper" data-rk-askable="true">' in host(spec, 'paper', askable=1)

save writes a page to a file. With linked fonts, it copies the font files beside it, so the file works from file://.


source

save
def save(
    specs, path, fonts:str='link', **kw
)->pathlib.Path:
Write page(specs) to path; with fonts='link', copy the fonts to fonts/ beside it.



import tempfile


out = save(spec, Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())/'t.html')
assert (out.parent/'fonts'/'literata-latin-wght-normal.woff2').exists()

FastHTML: Demo and Assets
Demo(spec) is the host element as an FT component. Assets(prefix) gives the Link and the Script for a server that serves the bundle at prefix. A server that shows scenes also serves bundle('three') as three.js at the same prefix. The runtime loads it from there the first time that a scene mounts, and only then.


source

Assets

The style and the script of the runtime, served at prefix; v busts the cache.




source

Demo

The host element of spec for a FastHTML page; theme='paper' gives it the paper look, askable the host switch.



x = to_xml(Demo(dict(id='d', ask='a </script> b')))
assert '<script type="application/json">' in x and 'data-rupaka' in x and 'a \\u003c/script> b' in x
assert 'data-rk-theme="paper"' in to_xml(Demo(dict(id='d'), theme='paper')) and 'data-rk-theme' not in x

assert 'data-rk-askable' not in x

version

A short hash of the script and the style.



test_eq(len(version()), 10)

title: agent
text:
author(concept, ask) asks a model for one demo on a concept. The model writes data only: a JSON spec. It never writes code. Then the loop checks the spec, and gives the errors back to the model to fix:
ask(prompt, sp) is any function that returns text, as in abhyasa. The tests use a fake one.

title: agent
text:
The catalog
The prompt lists the blocks and fns from their manifests, so it never names a block that the runtime does not have.


source

catalog
def catalog()->str:
The blocks and fns, with their purpose and props, as text for the prompt.


The catalog names every block and every fn.

cat = catalog()
for n in [*manifests(), *fn_manifests()]: assert f'- {n}: ' in cat, n
print(cat[:600])

title: agent
text:
The system prompt
The system prompt says who the demo is for, gives the rules of a good demo, the shape of a spec, and the catalog. The demo is for a human learner, who can be new to the idea or know it well. A demo that only restates the definition teaches little. So the prompt asks for a concrete case first, a picture of it next, and the general rule last (concreteness fading).


source

demo_sp
def demo_sp()->str:
The system prompt of the demo agent.



assert 'You never write code' in demo_sp() and '- wheel: ' in demo_sp()
assert 'Who this is for' in demo_sp() and 'Never only restate the definition' in demo_sp()

title: agent
text:
The user prompt
The user prompt describes the concept, the first error of the learner (if there is one), and two gallery demos as examples. The host can also give the learner’s level as a short text, for example “new to this” or “knows linear algebra”. With no level, the prompt does not change. near picks the gallery demos that share the most words with the concept. A long table in an example is cut to three rows.


source

near
def near(
    concept, k:int=2
)->list:
The k gallery demos that share the most words with concept.




source

demo_prompt
def demo_prompt(
    concept, first_error:str='', examples:tuple=(), level:str=''
)->str:
The prompt that asks for a demo on concept, a dict with name, statement, subject and misconceptions.



c = dict(name='Reciprocal rank fusion', statement='Sum 1/(k + rank) over the lists.', subject='ml', misconceptions=['raw scores add'])
p = demo_prompt(c, 'You add the raw scores.', near(c))
assert 'first error: You add the raw scores.' in p and '"id": "reciprocal-rank-fusion"' in p

A level, when the host gives one, goes into the prompt. With no level, the prompt is the same as before.

assert "The learner's level: new to ranking." in demo_prompt(c, level='new to ranking')
test_eq(demo_prompt(c), demo_prompt(c, level=''))
assert 'level' not in demo_prompt(c)

title: agent
text:
The repair prompt
The repair prompt gives back the spec and only its errors. It tells the model to keep the teaching text, so a repair does not make the words more literal.


source

repair_prompt
def repair_prompt(
    spec, errors
)->str:
The prompt that asks the model to fix only errors in spec.

title: agent
text:
Parse
parse_json finds the JSON object in a reply, also inside a fence or after some text.


source

parse_json
def parse_json(
    s:str
)->dict:
The first JSON object in s. Raise ValueError when there is none.



test_eq(parse_json('Here:\n```json\n{"a": 1}\n```'), {'a': 1})
test_fail(lambda: parse_json('no json'), contains='no JSON')

title: agent
text:
author
author runs the loop. It stamps the spec with the schema, an id and the concept slug. log, when given, gets one entry for each failed try. level goes on to demo_prompt.


source

author
def author(
    concept, ask, first_error:str='', examples:NoneType=None, check:bool=True, repairs:int=2, log:list=None,
    level:str=''
)->dict | None:
A checked demo spec on concept from the model ask, or None after repairs failed repairs. A spec with texts that are not plain (plain_errors) gets one repair; the plainer good spec stays.



Tests with a fake model
fake replies from a list, one reply for each call, and keeps the prompts.

from rupaka.spec import examples as block_examples


def fake(*replies):
    calls = []
    def ask(p, sp=''): calls.append(p); return replies[min(len(calls), len(replies)) - 1]
    ask.calls = calls
    return ask
good = json.dumps(block_examples()['gate'])

A good spec passes on the first call. The spec gets the concept slug.

a = fake(good)
s = author(dict(name='Sums', slug='sums'), a, check=False)
test_eq((s['concept'], len(a.calls)), ('sums', 1))

A spec with one error gets one repair. The repair prompt names the error.

broken = json.loads(good); del broken['blocks'][1]['after']
a, log = fake(json.dumps(broken), good), []
s = author('Sums', a, check=False, log=log)
assert s is not None and len(a.calls) == 2
assert 'gives away the answer of gate "sum"' in a.calls[1] and 'Fix only these errors' in a.calls[1]
test_eq(log[0]['tries'], 1)

author gives the level on to the prompt.

a = fake(good)
author('Sums', a, check=False, level='an expert')
assert "The learner's level: an expert." in a.calls[0]

Three bad replies give up quietly: the result is None, and the log has three entries.

log = []
test_eq(author('Sums', fake('not json', json.dumps(broken), '{}'), check=False, log=log), None)
test_eq(len(log), 3)

A model that fails gives up too, with no exception.

def down(p, sp=''): raise ConnectionError('no network')
test_eq(author('Sums', down, check=False), None)

A good spec with a text that is not plain gets one repair. The repair prompt names the problem, and the plainer spec comes back.

vague = json.loads(good); vague['ask'] = 'This departs from the usual rule.'
a, log = fake(json.dumps(vague), good), []
s = author('Sums', a, check=False, log=log)
test_eq((s['ask'], len(a.calls)), (json.loads(good)['ask'], 2))
assert '"departs from" is vague' in a.calls[1]

When the repair is not plainer, or does not pass the checks, the first good spec stays. The plain check never costs a demo.

test_eq(author('Sums', fake(json.dumps(vague)), check=False)['ask'], vague['ask'])
test_eq(author('Sums', fake(json.dumps(vague), 'not json', 'not json'), check=False)['ask'], vague['ask'])

With a browser, check runs too, and a good spec still passes in one call.

from rupaka.check import can_check


if can_check(): assert author('Sums', fake(good)) is not None

title: agent
text:
Plain English
A host can make a text plain with plain. When plain_why finds problems in a text, plain asks the model once to write it again, and names the problems. It keeps the new text only when it has fewer problems and keeps each number, each $...$ maths span and each code span. Else the old text stays. A text that passes costs no call. A dict of texts costs at most one call for all the texts that fail.


source

plain_prompt
def plain_prompt(
    x, why
)->str:
The prompt that asks the model to write x (a text, or a dict of texts) again; why has the problems (of each key, for a dict).


keeps says whether a new text keeps the maths, the code and the numbers of the old text, and each text of keep that the old text has.


source

keeps
def keeps(
    old:str, new:str, keep:tuple=()
)->bool:
Whether new has each maths span, code span, number and keep text of old.



assert keeps('Add $a+b$ to 3 apples.', 'You have 3 apples. Add $a+b$.')
assert not keeps('Add $a+b$ to 3 apples.', 'You have 4 apples. Add $a+b$.')
assert not keeps('Run `f(x)`. Check: why?', 'Run f(x). Check: why?') and not keeps('Check: why?', 'Why?', keep=['Check:'])

plain takes a text or a dict of texts. A new text must also look like a text: not empty, not JSON in place of words, and not less than a third of the old length, and not more than about three times it.


source

plain
def plain(
    ask, x, terms:tuple=(), keep:tuple=()
):
x (a text, or a dict of texts) in plain English: each text that fails plain_why is written again by ask in one call, and kept only when it is better.


A text that passes makes no call. The owner’s bad question gets one call, and the plain version comes back.

good_q = 'In a DDPM, the amount of noise at each step is set before training. Suppose the network learns this amount instead. Which DDPM rule does this break? Why?'
bad_q = 'You train a DDPM on recordings of rain. You ask the network to learn the noise recipe as it trains. Why does this depart from a DDPM simplifying assumption?'
a = fake(good_q)
test_eq((plain(a, good_q), len(a.calls)), (good_q, 0))
test_eq((plain(a, bad_q), len(a.calls)), (good_q, 1))
assert '"recipe" is a nickname' in a.calls[0]

A new text that drops a number or the maths, or that is not better, is not kept. A model that fails keeps the old text too.

q = 'The loss is $L = (y - 3)^2$; it uses 3 as the target and you facilitate the fit.'
test_eq(plain(fake('The loss is $L$. It uses a target.'), q), q)
test_eq(plain(fake(q), q), q)
test_eq(plain(down, q), q)
new = 'The loss is $L = (y - 3)^2$. It uses 3 as the target. You help the fit.'
test_eq(plain(fake(new), q), new)

A dict sends only the texts that fail, in one call, and keeps the others as they are.

a = fake(json.dumps(dict(q=good_q)))
test_eq(plain(a, dict(q=bad_q, o='Yes.')), dict(q=good_q, o='Yes.'))
test_eq(len(a.calls), 1); assert '"o"' not in a.calls[0]

title: agent
text:
A live run
A live run uses a real model, so it is not part of the tests. With the rishi package and its model claude/sonnet, it looks like this:
from rishi import Chat, resp_text
def ask(p, sp=''):
    chat = Chat('claude/sonnet', sp=sp)
    try: return resp_text(chat(p))
    finally: chat.close()
log = []
spec = author(dict(name='Guṇa sandhi', statement='a or ā before i, u or ṛ gives e, o or ar.', subject='sanskrit'), ask, log=log)
The first live run (26 October 2026, claude/sonnet, three concepts: guṇa sandhi, cosine similarity and binary search):








concept
result
model calls




guṇa sandhi
passed on the first try

title: rupaka
text:
rupaka (रूपक) means a form, a play that the audience sees, and the figure of speech that shows one thing through another.
A rupaka demo is one interactive figure that teaches one idea. You write it as a JSON spec of small blocks: sliders, plots, 3D scenes, flows, and a gate that asks the learner to predict first. Python checks the spec (validate), and a small runtime draws it in the browser with no network. A model can write a spec for you (author), because a spec cannot run code.

title: rupaka
text:
Install
uv add rupaka        # or: pip install rupaka
The headless check (check) needs playwright: uv add "rupaka[check]". It uses the Chromium that playwright install chromium gives, or the browser in $FASTCDP_CHROME. It never runs your everyday Chrome.

title: rupaka
text:
A demo in one minute
Build the spec with the Python builders. You can also write the same thing as JSON.

from rupaka.spec import *

This demo asks for a sum. The answer and the sliders wait for the prediction.

d = demo('sum', 'Add two numbers', ask='Predict the sum before you see it.', state=dict(a=2, b=3), derive=[expr('a + b', 'sum')],
         blocks=[gate('s', 'What is {a} + {b}?', [4, 5, 6], 'sum', why='Say why, in one line.', context='For a = {a} and b = {b}:'),
                 readout('{a} + {b} = {sum}', after='s'),
                 row(slider('a', 'a', 0, 9, 1, lock='s'), slider('b', 'b', 0, 9, 1, lock='s'))])

validate gives the errors. An empty list means that the spec is good.

assert validate(d) == []

A readout that shows the sum before the gate breaks the think rule, so validate refuses it:

bad = {**d, 'blocks': [d['blocks'][0], readout('{a} + {b} = {sum}')]}
assert any('wait' in e or 'after' in e for e in validate(bad))

save(d, 'sum.html') writes one page that works from file://. Open it in a browser. Before the lock in, the sum is hidden. After it, the learner sees the result and can move the sliders:







before the prediction
after the prediction









The page functions are in rupaka.render:

from rupaka.render import *

page(d) gives the same page as a string:

assert '<script' in page(d)

title: rupaka
text:
More examples

Predict, then move a slider
A plot of a curve. The lowest point and the caption wait for the gate, and the slider is locked until the lock in. The animation at the top of this page is this demo.

p = demo('parabola', 'What b does to a parabola', ask='The curve is y = x² + b·x. Now b = 0, so the lowest point is at the origin.',
         state=dict(b=0), derive=[expr('x^2 + b * x', 'curve', over=dict(x=[-5, 5, 101])), expr('-b / 2', 'vx'), expr('-(b^2) / 4', 'vy')],
         blocks=[axis([-5, 5], plot('curve'), point(x='vx', y='vy', label='lowest', after='move'), y=[-6, 10], height=300),
                 gate('move', 'b goes from 0 to 2. Where does the lowest point move?', ['Left and down', 'Right and down', 'It stays'],
                      is_('Left and down'), hides=['vx', 'vy']),
                 slider('b', 'b', -4, 4, 0.5, lock='move'),
                 caption('The lowest point is at x = −b / 2 = **{vx:2}**. Set b to −2. Where does the point go now?', after='move')])
assert validate(p) == []



A 3D scene
A scene holds bodies, forces, labels and camera shots. The force arrow shows the answer, so it waits for the gate.

s = demo('lift', 'Twice the weight', state=dict(step=1, cam='wide', w=4), derive=[expr('w * 2', 'up')],
         blocks=[gate('g', 'What is twice {w}?', [6, 8], 'up'),
                 scene(body('base', 'box', [2, 1, 2]), force([0, 1, 0], 'up', on='base', at=[0, 1.5, 0], label='lift, {up}', after='g'),
                       shot(bind='cam'), shot('close:base', step=2), bind='step', steps=['A box.', 'Look closer.'])])
assert validate(s) == []




A box with a lift arrow after the prediction




A worked example and a flow
An explainer (mode='learn') has no gate. It builds one step at a time: the host moves on with Rupaka.set(el, {step: n}). A pair is one row of a worked example, and a flow is a few boxes with arrows. page(panel, theme='paper') gives the paper look.

panel = demo('targets', 'Make a question and its answer', mode='learn', state=dict(step=1),
             blocks=[pair(['[18]'], '47', heads=['Input tensor', 'Target'], step=1), pair(['[18, 47]'], '56', step=2),
                     flow([dict(id='g', text='Guess'), dict(id='c', text='Compare'), dict(id='a', text='Adjust')], step=3)])
assert validate(panel) == []




Two rows of a worked example and a flow of three boxes, on paper




A board with a side panel
rupaka.board is the board of the screen guide. A model writes one JSON line for each mark: a step with a spoken line, marks on the page, and a side panel. parse_board checks each line against what the page has. A bad line drops. The model never sends HTML or script.

from rupaka.board import parse_board, clean_context

The page tells the board its parts (anchors). Here it has one passage:

text = 'A search engine splits the query into words. It finds the pages that match and makes a ranked list. Then it shows the top results.'
ctx = clean_context(dict(anchors=[dict(id='p1', kind='passage', text=text)]))

Each step says one line, marks the passage and adds boxes to a flow in the side panel:

lines = """{"op": "step", "say": "First the engine splits the query into words."}
{"op": "underline", "at": {"a": "p1", "text": "splits the query into words"}}
{"op": "panel", "head": "How a search works"}
{"op": "node", "id": "q", "text": "Query"}
{"op": "node", "id": "w", "text": "Words"}
{"op": "edge", "from": "q", "to": "w"}
{"op": "step", "say": "Then it finds the pages that match and makes a ranked list."}
{"op": "circle", "at": {"a": "p1", "text": "ranked list"}}
{"op": "node", "id": "p", "text": "Pages that match"}
{"op": "edge", "from": "w", "to": "p"}
{"op": "node", "id": "r", "text": "Ranked list"}
{"op": "edge", "from": "p", "to": "r"}
{"op": "step", "say": "Last, it shows the top results."}
{"op": "box", "at": {"a": "p1", "text": "the top results"}}
{"op": "node", "id": "t", "text": "Top results"}
{"op": "edge", "from": "r", "to": "t"}"""
board = parse_board(lines, ctx)
assert len(board.steps) == 3 and not board.dropped

The page draws it with rupakaBoard.play(board), from the script rupaka.board.bundle('js') and the style bundle('css'):



The board marks the passage and draws a flow in the side panel


A panel can also be a table, a list, a faded example with blanks, a card of a wrong idea, or three stages (see the board docs).


Plain English
plain_why finds the parts of a text that are hard to read: long sentences, a reading grade over 9, semicolons, vague words and nicknames. It needs no model.

why = plain_why('The model, which was trained on a very large amount of text from many sources over many weeks, uses attention; it is good.')
assert any('semicolon' in w for w in why) and any('grade' in w for w in why)

plain_errors(spec) checks all the texts of a demo.

assert plain_errors(d) == []

section: Make a demo with a model
text:
Make a demo with a model
author(concept, ask) asks a model for a demo, then validates it, plays it in a headless browser and repairs it. ask(prompt, sp) is any function that sends a prompt and a system prompt to a model and gives back text. For example, with the rishi package:
from rishi import Chat, resp_text
from rupaka.agent import author
spec = author('compound interest', lambda p, sp: resp_text(Chat('claude/sonnet', sp=sp)(p)))
author gives a spec that passes all the checks, or None. See the agent docs for a live run.

title: rupaka
text:
The blocks



block
what it does




gate
asks one question and hides the result until the learner locks in a prediction


readout
shows one large line from a template, for example {a} + {b} = {sum}


caption
explains the result after the reveal, and ends with a new question


slider, toggle, choice
change a number, turn a thing on or off, pick one case


wheel, ranklist
pick one item on a ring; drag rows to change an order


axis, plot, point
axes with a curve or dots, and a dot that the learner can drag


bars, grid, pixels
bars of a list, a heatmap, a grey image of rows of numbers


row, stack
put blocks side by side, or one above the other as one group


pair, flow
one row of a worked example; a few boxes with arrows


scene, body, force, label3d, shot
a 3D view, its parts, its arrows, its labels and its cameras



Each block has a manifest (rupaka/blocks/<name>/block.json) and an example. examples() gives the example of each block by name, and the spec docs have all the props.

title: rupaka
text:
More

How a demo teaches
A demo never shows the answer first. Each demo follows one loop:

Predict. The demo shows the inputs and asks one question. The result is hidden.
Reveal. The learner locks in with ⌘↩︎. The demo shows the result and says if the prediction was right.
Manipulate. Now the controls are live. The result changes when the inputs change.
Explain. The caption ends with a new question that the learner answers with the controls.

The validator enforces step 1: a block that shows a value which the answer depends on must wait for the gate. An explainer is the one exception. It has "mode": "learn" and no gate, so it shows a thing at once (see Explainers below).


What a demo is
A demo is a JSON spec, not code. It has a small state, derived values from named functions (fns), and a list of blocks. A model can write a spec safely, because a spec cannot run code.



part
what it is




block
a reusable UI part in rupaka/blocks/<name>/: its JS, its CSS, a block.json manifest and an example


fn
a pure function that computes a derived value: rules, rrf, softmax, lookup, expr, field, ids, pick, sort, fmt


gate
the block that asks for the prediction and hides the result until the lock in


spec
the JSON object: state, derive, blocks and tables, a mode that is predict (the default) or learn, and askable (true by default)





The host API
A host page can read and change a demo that it mounted. In these calls, el is the element that holds the demo: the [data-rupaka] element, or the element that you gave to Rupaka.mount.



call
what it does




Rupaka.state(el)
gives a copy of the input keys (the keys of spec.state) and their values


Rupaka.set(el, state)
sets the input keys that state has, then runs derive one time and draws one time. It ignores other keys.


Rupaka.options(el, gate)
gives the option values of the gate gate, in the order that the gate shows them. Each value is the value itself, not the text that the gate shows. The gate reads options from the state after derive, and this call does the same. An unknown gate gives null.


Rupaka.settle(el, gate, pick, {answer})
closes the gate gate as if the learner picked pick. It draws the verdict and shows the blocks that wait for the gate. With pick null, the gate closes with no verdict. An unknown gate does nothing and gives false. The options object is optional.


Rupaka.open(el, gate)
opens the closed gate gate again, as the Try another button of the gate does. It removes the pick, the reason and the verdict, and hides the blocks that wait for the gate. It draws one time. It does not move the focus. A gate that is open does not change, and the call gives true. A gate that waits for the host to save a prediction does not open, and the call gives false. An unknown gate does nothing and gives false.


Rupaka.mount(el, spec, {save, askable})
calls save(state) after each change of an input key. state is the value that Rupaka.state(el) gives. askable turns the Ask about this control on or off (see Host events).


Rupaka.ask(el, text)
sends the rk-ask event, as the Ask about this control does, for example from a voice command. It gives false when a listener called preventDefault.


Rupaka.append(el, block, {into})
adds one block at the end of the demo, or at the end of the stack or row at the path into, with no rebuild. The parts that show stay. It gives the path of the new block, for example 'blocks.3'. An unknown block type or a bad into throws an error.


Rupaka.anchor(el, path)
gives the element of the block or the part at path, or null. Each block has data-rk-id: its path in the spec, such as 'blocks.2'. A part adds to it: 'blocks.2.cells.0', 'blocks.2.to', 'blocks.3.nodes.1'. The element can be hidden, for example in a later step.



Rupaka.set, Rupaka.settle and Rupaka.open never send rk-predict, never add to st.log and never call save. Rupaka.options only reads. A lock does not stop Rupaka.set. Each call throws an error when no demo is mounted in el.
To show one demo in two windows, mount the spec in each window. Send Rupaka.state of the first copy to the second window, and call Rupaka.set there. To send a pick, send its index in Rupaka.options of the first copy. In the second window, find the value at that index in Rupaka.options, and call Rupaka.settle with it. When the learner in the first window clicks Try another, call Rupaka.open in the second window.
A host can remove the gate answers from the spec of a copy that a room sees, so that the room cannot read them early. Then give the answer to Rupaka.settle in answer. The gate uses it to draw the verdict. answer is {is: value} or a path in the state, as in a gate. When the spec has an answer, the gate uses the answer in the spec. Rupaka does not write answer into the spec or the state. When the spec has no answer and you give no answer, the gate closes with no verdict.
rupaka.poll makes a question for a room from a gate. of_gate(spec, gate) gives the question and the index of the answer. public(p) gives the part that the room sees.


Host events
A demo sends two events to the host page. Each event bubbles, crosses a shadow root and is cancelable. In each event, detail.demo is the id of the spec.



event
when
detail




rk-predict
the learner locks in a prediction
gate, picked, ans, ok, why, context and settle(saved, message). A host that saves the prediction calls preventDefault, then calls settle.


rk-ask
the learner clicks Ask about this, or the host calls Rupaka.ask
text: the words of the learner (at most 500 characters, can be empty). state: the input keys and their values now, clipped. step: the state key step of an explainer, else the id of the first open gate, else null.



An rk-ask event is plain JSON. It never holds derived values, gate answers, DOM or HTML. A string in state has at most 200 characters, and a list or an object at most 50 items, 3 levels deep. A host that takes the ask calls preventDefault. Then the demo says “Sent to the tutor.”, else “No tutor is on this page.” For example:
document.addEventListener('rk-ask', e => { e.preventDefault(); tutor.ask(e.detail); });
// e.detail: {demo: 'add-two', text: 'explain this at b = 2', state: {a: 1, b: 2}, step: 'sum'}
The Ask about this control is on by default. A spec turns it off with "askable": false. A host page can turn it on or off for one render, and the host switch comes first. For example, a talk shows the control in the editor, but not in the window that the room sees. host, page and Demo take askable=True or askable=False, which writes data-rk-askable on the element. Rupaka.mount takes {askable}. The event is the same in every case.


3D scenes
A scene block draws a physical thing in 3D: a jet that hovers, a gearbox, a molecule. It holds four kinds of part:



block
what it is




body
a primitive (box, cylinder, cone, sphere, capsule, torus) or a group. in puts a body in another body, so a compound part moves as one. A state key in rot turns it


force
an arrow on a body. Its length is mag times the scene scale, so arrows compare. mag can be a state key or a derived key


label3d
a chip on a point, with a leader line. Chips never overlap: each chip goes to a free place around its point


shot
a named camera: wide, side, front, top or close:<body id>. The scene finds the framing from the bounds of what shows



The scene has a toon look: flat colours in three soft bands, ink outlines, a soft floor and a contact shadow. The colours come from the page theme, in light and dark. With bind, a scene builds one step at a time: a part with step: n shows from step n, and the camera moves to the newest shot. With prefers-reduced-motion, the camera cuts and parts show at once. The think rule holds: a force or a label that shows the answer of a gate must wait for the gate.
rupaka keeps a copy of three.js (0.185.0, MIT) in rupaka/static/vendor/three/. It loads only for a spec that has a scene, and never from a CDN:

page, save, show and md(frame=True) put three.js in the page when a spec has a scene, so the page works offline and from file://.
A server that serves the runtime at a prefix also serves bundle('three') as three.js at that prefix, beside rupaka.js. The runtime loads it from there the first time that a scene mounts. A host that serves it at another place sets Rupaka.base before the first scene mounts.


Scenes and the board
The board of the screen guide speaks one line for each step. It drives a scene with the host API, so “again”, “slower” and “next” need no new code:



board operation
host call




{"op": "step", "n": 3} with a scene spec
Rupaka.set(el, {step: 3}), where step is the bind of the scene


{"op": "demo", "set": {...}}
Rupaka.set(el, {...}), for example a slider value or a step


{"op": "cam", "shot": "side"}
Rupaka.cam(el, 'side'). It sets the key that a shot block binds. It gives false for a bad name, or when the scene has no bound shot



shots(spec) gives the shot names that a spec knows, so a host can check a cam operation before it draws. Each scene element also tells its state: data-rk-shot is the shot now, and data-rk-still is 1 when nothing moves.


Explainers
Sometimes the learner must see a thing before there is a good question, for example how a jet hovers. An explainer shows a scene at once, with no prediction step. Set "mode": "learn" on the spec. Then validate lets the spec have no gate. All the other checks still run.

An explainer cannot have a gate, and no block can wait for a gate or lock to a gate. validate refuses each one and says what to remove.
With no mode, or with "mode": "predict", a spec with no gate is refused as before. A mode that is not predict or learn is refused.
The runtime shows a small “Explainer” label above the title, so the learner knows that there is no prediction step. The .rk element has data-rk-mode="learn".

ex = demo('box', 'A box', mode='learn', state=dict(step=1), blocks=[scene(body('b', 'box', [1, 1, 1]), bind='step', steps=['A box.'])])


Panels that build with a voice
A board panel shows a worked example one row at a time, while a voice speaks. Use an explainer with the state key step:

A block with "step": n shows when the step is n or more, and draws in from the left. The host moves on with Rupaka.set(el, {step: n}).
A pair is one row: input cells, an arrow and the answer, for example [18] → 47. Its cells come in one by one, 80 ms apart.
A flow is two to five nodes with at most eight arrows, in a row or a cycle.
A server can stream the panel. It sends the start of the spec, then one block at a time. append(spec, block) checks each block in Python, and Rupaka.append(el, block) adds it in the page.
Rupaka.anchor(el, path) gives the element of a part, so the board can draw a curve from a mark on the page to that part.
theme='paper' on host, page or Demo (the attribute data-rk-theme="paper") gives a warm paper ground, light boxes, sketch lines and a hand font, Patrick Hand (OFL).




The screen-guide board
rupaka.board is the board of the screen guide. A learner says “I don’t get X”, and a model answers with a board: one short spoken line for each step, and marks on the page (a circle, a box, an arrow, a label, a sketch on a figure) and a small worked example in a side panel. abhyasa and Leela both use it.

The model writes JSON lines in a closed language (OPS). parse_board(text, ctx) checks each line against the page context: a bad line drops, and two bad lines in a row end the board. The model never sends HTML, script or a link.
clean_context(raw) keeps only the known keys of what the page sends (its anchors, the focus, the thread and the demo) and cuts them to size.
stream_board(chunks, ctx, on_step) gives each step to the page as soon as it is whole.
static/board.js draws a checked board as window.rupakaBoard.play(board). The side panel is on the paper of the demos, in the hand font. A host serves bundle('js'), bundle('css') and the pen libraries in assets().libs.

The decisions about learning (when the tutor is sure, which sources to trust, the prompts) stay in the app.


Develop
The notebooks in nbs/ are the source of the Python. The JS and CSS are hand-written files under rupaka/static/, rupaka/blocks/ and rupaka/fns/.
uv sync
uv run nbdev-prepare
uv run pytest

title: poll
text:
A presenter can ask a room the question of a demo gate. of_gate makes a choice question from the gate, with no model call. public keeps the part of a question that the room sees.
abhyasa and Leela share this module. abhyasa had the same contract first, as abhyasa.talk.ask_from_gate and public_ask.

title: poll
text:
A path in the state
_at reads a path such as fused.0.id in the state. A path that is not in the state gives _NONE, so a value of None is not the same as no value. It reads own keys only, as the runtime does: __proto__, prototype and constructor give _NONE.
A path reads into lists, and a missing key gives _NONE:

st = dict(a=None, xs=[dict(id='p')], constructor=1)
assert _at(st, 'a') is None and _at(st, 'xs.0.id') == 'p'
assert _at(st, 'b') is _NONE and _at(st, 'xs.1') is _NONE and _at(st, 'constructor') is _NONE

title: poll
text:
A question from a gate
The options of a gate are a list, or {"from": path} in the state of the spec. The answer is {"is": value}, or a path in the state. of_gate reads the state of the spec and does not run derive. A path that needs derive gives None. Fewer than 2 or more than 6 options give None, and so does an answer that is not an option. The prompt gets the values of the state. A {name} with no value stays as it is.


source

of_gate
def of_gate(
    spec:dict, gate:str
)->dict | None:
A choice question from the gate gate of spec, with the index of the right option; None when the gate can not be a room question.


The gallery gates with fixed options and a fixed answer give a question. The gates that need derive give None, and so does an unknown gate.

g = gallery()
assert of_gate(g['parabola-vertex'], 'move') == dict(kind='choice', q='b goes from 0 to 2. Where does the lowest point move?',
                                                     options=['Left and down', 'Right and down', 'Straight up', 'It stays'], answer=0)
assert of_gate(g['reciprocal-rank-fusion'], 'win') is None   # the answer needs derive
assert of_gate(g['vowel-sandhi'], 'join') is None            # the options need derive
assert of_gate(g['softmax-temperature'], 'nope') is None

A gate in a row, with its options and its answer in the state:

spec = dict(state=dict(k=60, opts=['x', 'y'], best='y'), blocks=[dict(type='row', blocks=[dict(type='gate', id='g', prompt='With k = {k} and {m}?',
                                                                                         options={'from': 'opts'}, answer='best')])])
assert of_gate(spec, 'g') == dict(kind='choice', q='With k = 60 and {m}?', options=['x', 'y'], answer=1)

The prompt and the options show values as the demo shows them in the browser. 2.0 shows as 2, null shows as nothing, and a minus sign is a true minus:

spec = dict(state=dict(b=2.0, t=0.1, x=-1.5, z=-0.0, n=None, ok=True, p=1/3), blocks=[dict(type='gate', id='g', prompt='{b} {t} {x} {z} {n} {ok} {p} {p:2}',
                                                                                       options=[2.0, 0.1, 1.5, True], answer={'is': 2.0})])
test_eq(of_gate(spec, 'g'), dict(kind='choice', q='2 0.1 −1.5 0  true 0.3333 0.33', options=['2', '0.1', '1.5', 'true'], answer=0))

title: poll
text:
The part the room sees
public keeps the kind, the question, the options, and most (the most characters of a words answer). It drops the answer and the source.


source

public
def public(
    p:dict | None
)->dict | None:
The part of question p that the room sees: no answer and no source.


abhyasa adds src to a question from a gate. public drops it, and the answer:

a = dict(of_gate(g['softmax-temperature'], 'hot'), src=dict(demo='softmax-temperature', gate='hot'))
assert a == dict(kind='choice', q='T goes from 1 to 2. What happens to the share of Paris?',
                 options=['It rises', 'It falls', 'It stays the same'], answer=1, src=dict(demo='softmax-temperature', gate='hot'))
assert public(a) == dict(kind='choice', q='T goes from 1 to 2. What happens to the share of Paris?', options=['It rises', 'It falls', 'It stays the same'])
assert public(dict(kind='words', q='Say why.', most=80)) == dict(kind='words', q='Say why.', most=80)
assert public(None) is None

title: board
text:
A learner looks at a page and says “I don’t get alpha bar”. A tutor answers on the page, as a teacher does at a whiteboard. It circles the term, draws an arrow to a label in the figure, moves the slider of the demo, fills a small worked example in a side panel, and speaks one short line for each step.
This module is the part of the board that knows nothing about learning:
static/board.js draws a checked board on the page, and static/texparts.js gives a formula the ids of its parts. abhyasa and Leela both use this module and these files. The decisions about learning stay in abhyasa: the tutor tiers (tutor, then vault, then web), the trust rules of sources, and the prompts.
Import the helpers. The module needs only fastcore.

title: board
text:
The files
A host serves the files of the board. assets gives their paths. bundle('js') is texparts.js and board.js as one script, and bundle('css') is the paper tokens and board.css as one style sheet. The pen libraries (Rough.js and perfect-freehand, MIT) are in the folder libs. The board loads them on its first use from the URL folder host.assets (default /vendor/), so a host serves libs there. The board’s side panel uses the hand font Patrick Hand: a host loads it with rupaka.render.font_css.
The script sets window.rupakaBoard and window.rupakaTex. It sets the old names window.abhyasaBoard and window.abhyasaTex to the same objects, so a host that uses the old names works.


source

bundle
def bundle(
    kind:str='js'
)->str:
The board as one script (js) or one style sheet (css).




source

assets
def assets()->fastcore.basics.AttrDict:
The files of the board: js and css in bundle order, tex (the formula parts), and libs, the folder of the pen libraries and their licences.


Each file is in the package, and the script names the new global and the old one:

a = assets()
assert all(p.exists() for p in [*a.js, *a.css, a.tex]) and all((a.libs/f).exists() for f in (*LIBS, 'LICENSES.md'))
js = bundle()
assert 'window.rupakaBoard = window.abhyasaBoard' in js and 'window.rupakaTex = window.abhyasaTex' in js
assert '--rk-paper:' in bundle('css') and '.board-panel' in bundle('css')


The board language
A reply is JSON lines: one object on each line. The server checks each line alone, so a bad line drops and the rest draws. There are 17 commands. The model never writes HTML, CSS, script or a URL.



op
fields
what it does




step
say, and src with quote
starts a step; say is the spoken line. A quote is word for word from source src


circle, box, underline
at
a hand-drawn ring, box or line on the anchor


arrow
from, to
a curved arrow between two anchors


label
at, text, side
a short note beside the anchor


sketch
at, pts
a free line in the box of a figure anchor, to mark a part of the figure


point
at
moves a pointer mark to the anchor


clear
n (optional)
removes the marks of all steps, or of step n


demo_set
set
changes inputs of the step’s rupaka demo, only after its gate is open


video_at
t, quote
moves the explainer video to t seconds, and quotes its transcript there


panel
title, head, cols, numbered, stages (each optional)
starts the side panel at the top right of the window: a small title, a bold heading and the names of two columns. With stages, its three rows are a case, a picture and the symbols. A new panel starts a new beat


row
cells, and to, at, chain (optional)
adds one row to the side panel: the cells as boxes, then an arrow and to. With at, the page circles that thing and a hand-drawn curve links it to the row. With chain, the cells are words with arrows between them. A cell {"blank": value} hides its value until the next step


note
text
one quiet line in the side panel


node
id, text
one box of a flow diagram in the side panel. id is a short name (a letter, then letters, digits or _)


edge
from, to, text (optional)
an arrow from box from to box to of the flow diagram, with a short label. An arrow back to an earlier box is a loop


myth
think, fact, why
a card of a wrong idea: “You might think” think, “In fact” fact, and one line of why



Each stroke can have w: the word of say where it starts.
A sketch marks a part of a figure only, so no shape covers the words of the page. A picture of an idea goes in the side panel. For a formula, the tutor gives an example from day-to-day life and marks the page’s own formula.
The side panel is the place for a small concrete example (Explain). The tutor builds it one row in each step, from the real values on the page: its row names the anchor of the value in at. The page circles the value and draws a curve from it to the row, so the model writes no circle for it. A process of 3 to 5 steps is a panel with numbered rows, or one chain row. A pipeline, a loop or a branch is a flow diagram: boxes (node) and arrows between them (edge), one box or two in each step, so the diagram grows with the talk.
Three more shapes come from the research on teaching. A faded worked example solves its first row, and each later row hides one more part as a blank, for the learner to fill: the blank shows its value when the next step plays, or when the learner clicks it. A wrong idea card (myth) puts a common wrong idea next to the right one, with one line of why. A panel with stages goes from the concrete to the abstract in three rows: a case, a picture (a chain), then the symbols. A new panel line starts the next beat, for example from the values on the page to the big idea. The side panel is the one picture of Explain. Show is a rupaka demo.
The first line can be a header: {"op":"v","n":1,"sure":0.9,"need":"none"}. sure is how sure the model is, from 0 to 1. need says what it needs to be sure: none, vault or web.


Anchors
A stroke names a thing on the page. The page sends a list of anchors, each with an id, a kind and its text. A formula also has its tokens (the TeX of its parts), a figure has its labels (a box for each label in the image), and the demo has its inputs.








form
example
the place




an id
"passage"
the whole anchor


words
{"a": "passage", "text": "closed form"}
the words in the anchor


a maths token
{"a": "m1", "tex": "\\bar\\alpha_t"}
the part of the formula


a figure label
{"a": "figure", "label": "a"}
the label in the image


a box
{"a": "figure", "box": [100, 200, 400, 600]}
a part of the anchor, from 0 to 1000


a point
{"a": "m1", "pt": [1100, 500]}
a point beside the anchor, for the far end of an arrow



Two ways to write the same TeX must match. norm_tex takes out the spaces and the braces around one symbol.

def norm_tex(
    s:str
)->str:
s with no white space, and with no braces around one character or one command, so \bar{\alpha}_{t} is \bar\alpha_t.


Braces and spaces do not change the match:

test_eq(norm_tex(r'\bar{\alpha}_{t}'), norm_tex(r'\bar\alpha_t'))
test_eq(norm_tex(r'\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}'), r'\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}')   # a group of two symbols keeps its braces
test_ne(norm_tex(r'\alpha_t'), norm_tex(r'\bar\alpha_t'))

Words match with no case and with white space made single, as the page shows them.

anchor_why
def anchor_why(
    at, ctx
)->str:
Why at names no anchor of ctx, or ’’ when it does.


A small context for the tests: a passage, the DDPM formula with its tokens, a triangle figure with labels a and b, and a demo with the input t.


source

by_id
def by_id(
    ctx
)->fastcore.basics.AttrDict:
ctx with by: its anchors by id.



DDPM = r'q(\mathbf{x}_t\mid\mathbf{x}_0)=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_t;\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\mathbf{x}_0,(1-\bar\alpha_t)\mathbf{I})'
ctx = by_id(dict(anchors=[dict(id='passage', kind='passage', text='It admits sampling x_t at an arbitrary timestep t in closed form.'),
                          dict(id='m1', kind='formula', text=DDPM, tokens=[r'\bar\alpha_t', r'\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}', r'\mathbf{x}_0', r'(1-\bar\alpha_t)']),
                          dict(id='out', kind='text', text='tensor([18]) gives 47. 1.0 and 1.0 give 1.414, and 2.0 gives 2.0. Guess, compare, then update the weights.'),
                          dict(id='figure', kind='figure', text='A right triangle', labels=dict(a=[100, 420, 160, 500], b=[480, 880, 540, 960]))],
                 demo=dict(inputs=dict(t=dict(value=500, min=0, max=1000, label='Step t')), open=False)))

Each form finds its anchor, and a wrong name does not:

test_eq(anchor_why('passage', ctx), '')
test_eq(anchor_why(dict(a='m1', tex=r'\bar{\alpha}_t'), ctx), '')
test_eq(anchor_why(dict(a='passage', text='Closed  form'), ctx), '')
test_eq(anchor_why(dict(a='figure', label='a'), ctx), '')
test_eq(anchor_why(dict(a='figure', box=[0, 0, 500, 500]), ctx), '')
assert anchor_why('e7', ctx)                                  # an id that the page did not send
assert anchor_why(dict(a='m1', tex=r'\beta_t'), ctx)          # a token that is not in the formula
assert anchor_why(dict(a='passage', text='open form'), ctx)   # words that are not in the passage
assert anchor_why(dict(a='figure', label='c'), ctx)           # a label that is not in the figure
assert anchor_why(dict(a='figure', box=[500, 0, 100, 10]), ctx)
assert anchor_why(dict(a='m1', tex=r'\bar\alpha_t', text='x'), ctx)   # two forms at once

Words mark a thing only when the page shows them in one place. A part of a word does not count, so “form” does not mark the “form” of “transform”. Words that are in the anchor two times drop, because the page cannot know which place the model means. Words inside a formula drop too: the page draws the formula as maths, so a mark goes on its part with tex.

tctx = by_id(dict(anchors=[dict(id='p', kind='passage', text='A transform maps symbol representations $(x_1, \\dots, x_n)$ to continuous representations $z$.')]))
test_eq(anchor_why(dict(a='p', text='continuous representations'), tctx), '')
test_eq(anchor_why(dict(a='p', text='form'), tctx), "no words 'form' in p")
test_eq(anchor_why(dict(a='p', text='representations'), tctx), "the words 'representations' are in p more than once")
test_eq(anchor_why(dict(a='p', text='x_1'), tctx), 'words inside a formula of p: mark its part with tex')
test_eq(anchor_why(dict(a='p', text='$z$'), tctx), 'words inside a formula of p: mark its part with tex')



The check of one line
check_line gives the reason that a line drops, or ''. Each string in a line is checked too: no tag, no script and no link can get in, also as the text of a label.
A cue of the explainer video is [t, text]. cue_at gives the cue that plays at t seconds. cue_quote finds a quote in the cue at t or in the cue before or after it. It gives the start of the cue where the quote begins, and the quote as the transcript says it. The board seeks the video to that start, so a time that the model gives a little late still lands on the right cue.


source

cue_quote
def cue_quote(
    cues, t:float, quote:str
):
(start, words) when quote (3 words or more) is word for word in the cue at t with the cue before and after it: the start of the cue where it begins, and the quote as the transcript says it. Else None.




source

cue_at
def cue_at(
    cues, t:float
):
The cue (start, text) that plays at t: the last one that starts at or before t. None when there is none.




source

check_line
def check_line(
    o, ctx
)->str:
Why the reply line o drops, or ’’ when it is good. ctx comes from by_id.




source

plain_say
def plain_say(
    say:str
)->str:
The spoken line say with no semicolon: each part is a sentence of its own.


Good lines pass. The checks drop an unknown op, an unknown key, a link and markup:

test_eq(check_line(dict(op='circle', at=dict(a='m1', tex=r'\bar\alpha_t'), w=0), ctx), '')
test_eq(check_line(dict(op='label', at=dict(a='figure', label='a'), text='side a', side='left'), ctx), '')
test_eq(check_line(dict(op='arrow', **{'from': dict(a='m1', pt=[1100, 500]), 'to': dict(a='m1', tex=r'(1-\bar\alpha_t)')}), ctx), '')
test_eq(check_line(dict(op='clear'), ctx), '')
assert check_line(dict(op='script', code='alert(1)'), ctx)
assert check_line(dict(op='circle', at='passage', html='<b>'), ctx)
assert check_line(dict(op='label', at='passage', text='see https://evil.example'), ctx)
assert check_line(dict(op='label', at='passage', text='<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>'), ctx)
assert check_line(dict(op='step', say='x' * 161), ctx)

A sketch marks a part of a figure, with at most 64 points. A sketch on another anchor drops: a picture of an idea goes in the side panel.

test_eq(check_line(dict(op='sketch', at=dict(a='figure', pt=[1050, 0]), pts=[[0, 0], [1000, 1000]]), ctx), '')
assert check_line(dict(op='sketch', at='figure', pts=[[i, i] for i in range(65)]), ctx)
test_eq(check_line(dict(op='sketch', at=dict(a='m1', pt=[1050, 0]), pts=[[0, 0], [1000, 1000]]), ctx), 'a sketch that is not on a figure')

A circle, a box, an underline or a label marks a thing on the page. On a bare point it has no thing under it, so it drops. A point and an arrow can use a point:

assert 'bare point' in check_line(dict(op='box', at=dict(a='passage', pt=[-200, 900])), ctx)
assert 'bare point' in check_line(dict(op='circle', at=dict(a='passage', pt=[500, 500])), ctx)
test_eq((check_line(dict(op='point', at=dict(a='passage', pt=[-200, 900])), ctx), check_line(dict(op='box', at=dict(a='passage', box=[0, 0, 500, 500])), ctx)), ('', ''))

The side panel: a panel line with its title, a row of short cells with an optional to and anchor, and a note. A number in a cell is good. A long cell, an empty row or an unknown anchor drops:

test_eq([check_line(o, ctx) for o in (dict(op='panel', title='tensors and targets', head='Make a question and its answer', cols=['Input', 'Target']),
                                       dict(op='row', cells=['[18]'], to=47, at=dict(a='passage', text='closed form')),
                                       dict(op='row', cells=['Guess', 'Compare', 'Adjust'], chain=True), dict(op='note', text='Both can be tensors.'))], [''] * 4)
for bad in (dict(op='row', cells=[]), dict(op='row', cells=['x' * 25]), dict(op='row', cells=['a'], at='e7'), dict(op='panel', cols=['a', 'b', 'c', 'd']),
            dict(op='note', text=''), dict(op='row', cells=['a'], chain='yes')): assert check_line(bad, ctx), bad

A flow diagram has boxes with a short id and arrows between them. A bad id, a long label and a word too long for a cell drop:

test_eq([check_line(o, ctx) for o in (dict(op='node', id='enc', text='Encoder'), dict(op='node', id='z', text='$\\mathbf{z}$'),
                                       dict(op='edge', **{'from': 'enc', 'to': 'z'}), dict(op='edge', **{'from': 'z', 'to': 'enc', 'text': 'back in'}))], [''] * 4)
test_eq(check_line(dict(op='node', id='1st', text='Encoder'), ctx), 'a bad box id')
test_eq(check_line(dict(op='edge', **{'from': 'a', 'to': 'b', 'text': 'a label that is far too long'}), ctx), 'a bad edge text')
test_eq(check_line(dict(op='row', cells=['Representations!'], to='z'), ctx), '')
test_eq(check_line(dict(op='row', cells=['Autoregressiveness'], to='z'), ctx), 'a word of more than 16 letters in a cell')
test_eq(check_line(dict(op='row', cells=[r'$\\mathrm{autoregressive}$'], to='z'), ctx), '')   # maths does not count

A cell can be a blank: {"blank": value} hides the value for the learner to fill. A card of a wrong idea has a short wrong idea, a short fact and one line of why:

test_eq(check_line(dict(op='row', cells=['[18, 47]'], to={'blank': 56}), ctx), '')
test_eq(check_line(dict(op='row', cells=[{'blank': {'blank': 1}}], to=2), ctx), 'bad cells')
test_eq(check_line(dict(op='myth', think='Alpha bar grows with t', fact='Alpha bar gets smaller with t', why='Each step keeps less of the picture.'), ctx), '')
test_eq(check_line(dict(op='myth', think='Alpha bar grows with t'), ctx), 'a bad wrong idea')
test_eq(check_line(dict(op='panel', head='From a case to symbols', stages=True), ctx), '')



Repair a panel line
A model often writes a panel line that is a little too long: an arrow label of a full sentence, a box with a second line, a note with a second sentence. When such a line drops, the picture breaks: a flow loses an arrow, and a panel loses its title. So repair_line makes the line good when one part of it is bad, and the rest of the line stays:

A panel line loses a bad title, head or column names.
An arrow loses a long label. The arrow is the structure of the flow; the label only names it.
A box keeps the first line of its text, or the name before a colon (Weight: a number to adjust is Weight).
A long note keeps its first whole sentences that fit. The maths markup does not count, only what shows.



source

repair_line
def repair_line(
    o, ctx
)->tuple:
(line, why): the side-panel line o that check_line drops, made good (see above), and why; else (None, '').


An arrow keeps its boxes and loses its long label. A box keeps its name. A note keeps the sentence that fits:

test_eq(repair_line(dict(op='edge', **{'from': 'out', 'to': 'dec', 'text': 'Earlier outputs guide the next choice'}), ctx),
        (dict(op='edge', **{'from': 'out', 'to': 'dec'}), 'a long label of an arrow: the label goes'))
test_eq(repair_line(dict(op='node', id='headA', text='Head A\nCompare Q with K, then mix V'), ctx)[0]['text'], 'Head A')
test_eq(repair_line(dict(op='node', id='w', text='Weight: the number that the model adjusts'), ctx)[0]['text'], 'Weight')
note = 'An example with our own numbers. Shops help to explain the roles, but real attention mixes vectors of numbers.'
test_eq(repair_line(dict(op='note', text=note), ctx)[0]['text'], 'An example with our own numbers.')

A panel line keeps its title when its head is too long, and a third column name is good. A good line, and a line with no part to cut, give None:

test_eq(repair_line(dict(op='panel', title='Roles', head='Rama serves rice to a child with a spoon from a pot in a garden'), ctx)[0], dict(op='panel', title='Roles'))
test_eq(check_line(dict(op='panel', cols=['Entries', 'Before', 'After']), ctx), '')
test_eq(repair_line(dict(op='note', text='Short.'), ctx), (None, ''))
test_eq(repair_line(dict(op='note', text='x' * 120), ctx), (None, ''))
test_eq(check_line(dict(op='note', text='$e^{1.414}\\approx4.113$ and $e^0=1$. Divide each by $5.113$ to get the shares of the two.'), ctx), '')   # 88 characters show

The demo gate: demo_set drops while the learner has not locked in a prediction, so the board cannot give the result first. After the lock-in it changes only inputs that the demo has, in their range.

assert 'gate' in check_line(dict(op='demo_set', set=dict(t=500)), ctx)
open_ctx = by_id({**ctx, 'demo': {**ctx.demo, 'open': True}})
test_eq(check_line(dict(op='demo_set', set=dict(t=500)), open_ctx), '')
assert check_line(dict(op='demo_set', set=dict(beta=1)), open_ctx)
assert check_line(dict(op='demo_set', set=dict(t=5000)), open_ctx)

video_at quotes the transcript at its time, word for word:

vctx = by_id({**ctx, 'video': dict(id='abc123def45', cues=[[0, 'Today we add noise.'], [61.5, 'Alpha bar is the share of the signal that is left.'], [70, 'It falls as t grows.']])})
test_eq(check_line(dict(op='video_at', t=63, quote='the share of the signal'), vctx), '')
assert check_line(dict(op='video_at', t=63, quote='the share of the noise'), vctx)
assert check_line(dict(op='video_at', t=63, quote='Alpha bar'), vctx)      # too short to be a quote
assert check_line(dict(op='video_at', t=63, quote='the share of the signal'), ctx)   # no video on the page

cue_quote gives the start of the cue that holds the quote, and the words as the transcript has them:

cs = vctx.video['cues']
test_eq(cue_quote(cs, 63, 'THE SHARE of the signal'), (61.5, 'the share of the signal'))
test_eq(cue_quote(cs, 71, 'share of the signal'), (61.5, 'share of the signal'))   # the time is late: the cue before holds it
test_eq(cue_quote(cs, 63, 'left. It falls'), (61.5, 'left. It falls'))             # a quote across two cues starts in the first
test_eq(cue_quote(cs, 5, 'the share of the signal'), (61.5, 'the share of the signal'))
assert cue_quote(cs, 200, 'Today we add noise.') is None                           # too far from its time



The whole reply
parse_board reads a reply line by line. Each step keeps at most 6 strokes, and a board has at most 6 steps. A stroke before the first step drops. Two dropped lines in a row end the board (failed): the steps before them stay. A dropped line of the side panel does not count for this: it is a long label or a long text, not a reply that went wrong.
A step can quote a source: src is the number of the source in ctx.sources, and quote must be word for word in its text, with 40 to 600 characters. verbatim checks it: white space is made single, and the quote goes from a word boundary to a word boundary. A host can give its own check as verbatim(quote, text) -> str (abhyasa gives the rules of its sources). A quote that fails drops, and the step stays, in the tutor’s words.


Each row with its step
A step says one thing, and its row and its marks show that same thing. So the spoken line of a step must name what its row shows. key_terms gives the key words and symbols of a text: each word of 3 letters or more that is not a small word, each number, and each maths token such as x_i. named is true when a row (or a note) and a spoken line share one of them. The check is cheap and knows no subject. page_terms gives the key terms of what the page shows.
The panel is an example. It can come from the page, or it can be the tutor’s own case (“deva + ālaya → devālaya” on a page that names no word). So parse_board drops a row that names no word of the page only when another row of its panel does, and when it shares no word with the other rows or the title and head of its panel: then it is the odd one out, such as a later idea at the end of a worked example. A row with only numbers or symbols, and a box of a flow diagram, never drop for this: a diagram with one box less is broken. Then it pairs each row, note and box with its step (_pair). A row that its own step does not name moves to the next step of its panel that names it. A row that no step names drops. A row never moves back to an earlier step, so a stream sends each row once, with the step that explains it.


source

page_terms
def page_terms(
    ctx
)->set:
The key terms of what the page shows: the text, tokens and labels of each anchor, the sources, and the demo.




source

named
def named(
    o, say:str
)->bool:
Whether the spoken line say names the panel line o (a row or a note): they share a key word or a symbol.




source

key_terms
def key_terms(
    s
)->set:
The key words and symbols of s: each word of 3 letters or more that is not a small word, cut to its first 5 letters; each number; each maths token such as x_i or w_1x_1; each single letter other than “a” and “I”. \sum counts as the word sum.




One shape for each panel
A panel is a table, a list or a flow diagram. Its lines line up only when they have one shape. A row is a pair (one or more cells, then an arrow and the answer to) or a chain (words with an arrow between each two). _shape sets the shape:

A flow diagram: the first line of the panel is a box (node). Its boxes and arrows (edge) stay, and rows drop. An arrow goes right after the later of its two boxes (_edges), and an arrow to a box that is not there drops.
A table: the panel has column names cols, and its first two rows are pairs with one cell less than the names and an answer. The names stand over the cells and the answers, so a later row that does not fit them drops. A chain of two words fits as one cell and its answer.
A list: else the names go and every row stays. A list lines up its chains on one grid, and the answer of a pair goes in the last column. Two short names say less than the rows, so the rows win.
A card of wrong ideas: the first line is a myth. It takes at most 2 of them, and no rows or boxes.
Three stages: a panel with stages is a list of at most 3 rows: a case, a picture, then the symbols. It has no column names.
A faded worked example: a row can hide parts as blanks. The first row of a panel shows its blanks, because it is the worked one.
At most 6 rows, 6 boxes and 8 arrows. More do not fit next to the page.

The first two rows decide, and not all of them, because a stream sends each row with its step: a later row cannot change the rows that show. So a stream holds a panel with column names until its second row is in (_held).

parse_board
def parse_board(
    text:str, ctx, verbatim:function=verbatim
)->fastcore.basics.AttrDict:
The checked board in the model’s reply text: steps, dropped lines with why, fixed lines with why (repair_line), hard spoken lines with their plain_why problems, sure, need and failed. verbatim checks a quote.

verbatim
def verbatim(
    quote:str, text:str
)->str:
quote with its white space made single, when it is in text word for word, from a word boundary to a word boundary, and has 40 to 600 characters; else ’’.

yt_link
def yt_link(
    vid:str, t:float
)->str:
The watch link that opens the video vid at t seconds, as fossick’s yt_link writes it.


The default check of a quote: white space does not count, a part of a word does not count, and a short quote does not count:

text = 'A notable property of the forward process is that it admits sampling x_t at an arbitrary timestep t in closed form.'
test_eq(verbatim('it admits  sampling x_t at an arbitrary timestep t in closed form', text), 'it admits sampling x_t at an arbitrary timestep t in closed form')
test_eq(verbatim('t admits sampling x_t at an arbitrary timestep t in closed form', text), '')

A board for “I don’t get alpha bar” on the DDPM formula: three steps, each with its strokes. The header says that the tutor is sure.

reply = '\n'.join(json.dumps(o) for o in [
    dict(op='v', n=1, sure=0.9, need='none'),
    dict(op='step', say='This formula adds noise in one jump.'), dict(op='box', at='m1', w=2),

The context
The page sends what it shows: its address, the step, the concept, the anchors, the demo, the video, and what the learner showed with the pointer (the focus), and the thread: the last questions on this page. clean_context keeps only the keys that it knows and cuts the text: at most 40 anchors, 300 characters an anchor and 6000 in all. An anchor id has only letters, digits and :_-. An unknown kind becomes text. A try anchor is the last graded try of the open check (see The learner’s answer): it keeps its own fields, each with its own bound (TRY). The result is a PageContext. A host cleans each context that is not one (abhyasa’s explain does), so a raw dict is cleaned too, even when it has a by key.

What the learner shows
While the learner talks or types the question, they can circle a part with the mouse, or hold the pointer still on it. The host finds the gestures and sends them as focus: a list of items, the latest first. Each item has a kind (circle or point), the anchors under it (the best one first), a box from 0 to 1000 of its first anchor, and t, the milliseconds from the start of the question. An item can have words: what the learner said or typed near that time.
_focus keeps at most 5 good items. It keeps only the anchor ids that the page sent, and drops an item with none of them, with a bad kind or with a bad box.


The thread of a page
A learner who asks “say that more simply” or “why?” after a board means that board. So the page keeps a short thread in memory, and sends it with the next question: the last 3 turns on this page, each with the question (said), the lines that its board said (says) and its tier (t). The page forgets the thread when the page changes, after 10 minutes with no question, or when the learner pushes Start fresh. The server keeps no thread: each question brings its own.
_thread keeps the good turns, the oldest first: a question of at most 300 characters, at most 6 lines of at most 160 characters, and a known tier. A turn with no question or no line drops, and so does a turn with a tag or a link in a line, which a board never says. At most 1500 characters stay in all: the oldest turn goes first.
The demo part keeps the inputs (with their value, range and label), the readouts, and whether the gate is open.

c = clean_context(dict(page='/walk/x/step/1', onload='x', anchors=[dict(id='passage', kind='passage', text='Some  text.'), dict(id='<b>', text='x')]))
test_eq(([a['id'] for a in c.anchors], c.anchors[0]['text'], 'onload' in c), (['passage'], 'Some text.', False))

A raw dict with a by key is not a PageContext, so a host cleans it. A cleaned context stays the same type:

test_eq((isinstance(c, PageContext), isinstance(dict(c), PageContext)), (True, False))

A circle on the formula and a point on the passage stay, the latest first. An unknown anchor id goes from its item:

shown = [dict(kind='circle', box=[100, 50, 400, 900], anchors=['m1', 'e7', 'passage'], t=2100.4, words='why is this  here'),
         dict(kind='point', box=[480, 480, 520, 520], anchors=['passage'], t=800)]
c = clean_context(dict(anchors=ctx.anchors, focus=shown))
test_eq(c.focus, [dict(kind='circle', box=[100, 50, 400, 900], anchors=['m1', 'passage'], t=2100, words='why is this here'),

Bad items drop: an unknown kind, no known anchor, a box that is not four finite numbers from 0 to 1000, and a box that is not a list:

bad = [dict(kind='lasso', box=[0, 0, 10, 10], anchors=['m1']), dict(kind='point', box=[0, 0, 10, 10], anchors=['e7']),
       dict(kind='point', box=[0, 0, float('nan'), 10], anchors=['m1']), dict(kind='point', box=[0, 0, 2000, 10], anchors=['m1']),
       dict(kind='point', box='0,0,10,10', anchors=['m1']), dict(kind='point', box=[5, 0, 5, 10], anchors=['m1']),
       dict(kind='point', box=[0, 0, 10, 10], anchors='m1'), 'circle']
test_eq('focus' in clean_context(dict(anchors=ctx.anchors, focus=bad)), False)
test_eq('focus' in clean_context(dict(anchors=ctx.anchors, focus='m1')), False)

At most 5 items stay, and each keeps at most 4 anchors:

many = [dict(kind='point', box=[0, 0, 10, 10], anchors=['m1', 'passage', 'figure', 'm1'], t=k) for k in range(8)]
c = clean_context(dict(anchors=ctx.anchors, focus=many))
